newsitem.title: UK: HSBC FX profits up as currency volatility grows. [CORRECTED 14:34 GMT]
newsitem.headline: HSBC FX profits up as currency volatility grows. [CORRECTED 14:34 GMT]

text.p: Foreign exchange performance at HSBC Holdings Plc improved in the first-half of 1997 as exchange-rate volatility increased, Guy Heald (Corrects from Held), treasurer at HSBC Midland said on Monday.
"Exchange-rate volatility was higher in the first half of the year and we have seen quite a lot more of customer business," Heald told Reuters.
HSBC Holdings, one of the world's biggest banking groups, said on Monday its foreign exchange profits rose 53 million pounds to 243 million pounds in the six-months to June 1997.

"I would say (FX) volumes are up quite dramatically in the first half of the year...There was a lot of activity, as you can imagine, in sterling," Heald said in a telephone interview following the release of first-half results.

Sterling has ballooned in 1997, pushing in late July to a high of 3.0878 marks per pound - the highest since August 1989 - on the back of a buoyant economy and hefty interest rates, one of the highest in Europe at around 6.75 percent.
Perceptions the euro could be a weak currency when it is launched have also helped boost the pound.

As well as sterling, Heald said activity this year has gravitated towards the yen and the emerging-market currencies where customers have sought to take action to protect themselves against exchange-rate fluctuations.

Currency markets, with daily turnover in excess of a trillion dollars, have gone wild in 1997. The U.S. dollar, involved in more than four-fifths of all currency trades, has been motoring higher for most of the year.
Dollar/mark on Monday, for instance, hit a high of 1.8730 and its highest since October 1989. Dollar/Swiss franc touched 47-month peaks around 1.5356.

Asian currencies have also been volatile. The Thai baht was hit by a de facto devaluation in May, which triggered a bout of volatility in the region - hitting the Philippine peso and Malaysian ringgit, to name but two, in its wake.
"We have seen in our overall customer business, naturally as a result of those exchange rates, interest by our customers in taking out cover against their exposures," said Heald.
"There has been an unusual level of volatility in some of those (Asian) currencies and I would imagine the central banks concerned will be quite concerned about reducing that volatility," he said.
Heald, however, said it would be impossible to forecast if the volatile trend on foreign exchange markets was set to continue.
"That (to predict) would be absolutely, absolutely impossible," he said.
While profit from HSBC's foreign exchange activity rose in the first half of 1997, dealing profits fell by 11 million to 296 million pounds, HSBC figures released on Monday showed.
First-half pre-tax profits at HSBC Holdings rose 13 percent to 2.623 billion pounds, compared with analysts' expectations mostly in a range of between 2.322 billion stg and 2.479 billion.
